analysis.one_liner: Gives Senate candidates public funds and cheaper ads if they accept campaign spending limits, while cutting PAC and party soft money.
analysis.headline: Feingold's Senate campaign spending limit and public financing bill was referred to the Senate Rules Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a voluntary system for Senate campaigns: a candidate who agrees to cap spending and limit contributions gets public money, discounted TV ads, and cheaper mailing rates from a fund financed by a $5 tax checkoff ($10 on joint returns). It also cuts the maximum PAC contribution from $5,000 to $1,000, bans national party committees from raising and spending unregulated 'soft money,' caps out-of-state contributions, requires bundlers to be disclosed, and restricts lobbyists' campaign fundraising. It was introduced January 21, 1997, referred to the Rules and Administration Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who get more disclosure of where campaign money comes from and less reliance on PAC and party soft-money channels; and Senate candidates who accept spending limits, who receive public financing, broadcast rates at 50 percent of the lowest unit charge, and discounted nonprofit mailing rates. Small-dollar in-state donors get more relative weight, since the bill requires half of a participating candidate's contributions to come from in-state residents.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and candidates who accept spending limits

how_it_helps.text: Candidates who accept spending limits get public financing payments from a new Senate Election Campaign Fund, funded by a $5-per-taxpayer checkoff, plus TV ad rates cut to half the lowest unit rate and nonprofit mailing rates [S2][S3].
The bill cuts the maximum contribution a PAC can make to a Senate candidate from $5,000 to $1,000 and caps total PAC money in a Senate race at $825,000 [S2][S3].

It prohibits national and congressional party committees from soliciting or spending soft money, and requires state party spending that could affect a federal election to come from federally regulated funds [S2].
Contributions delivered by bundlers must be reported as coming from the bundler as well as the original donor, and certain lobbyist solicitation of contributions is prohibited [S2].
Candidates who refuse the limits must state in their ads that they have not agreed to voluntary spending limits, and big-spending candidates face rapid reporting to their opponents [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees lose most of their ability to fund Senate campaigns, party committees lose their soft-money channel, broadcasters lose discounted-ad revenue, and wealthy candidates who want to finance their own campaigns with unlimited personal money are capped at $25,000. Taxpayers bear a small cost through the voluntary $5 checkoff.

drawbacks.text: Taxpayers pay for the public financing fund, though only through the voluntary $5 ($10 joint) checkoff added to tax returns, and payments shrink pro rata if the fund runs short [S2][S3].
Spending caps can favor incumbents, who start with name recognition and constituent contact, which is a standard objection to expenditure limits the bill's own supporters had to answer [S3].

The limits do not reach independent expenditures: a candidate facing $10,000 or more in outside spending simply gets permission to spend the same amount, so outside money remains an escape valve [S2].

The bill itself anticipates constitutional challenge: it provides for expedited Supreme Court review of any ruling on its constitutionality and voids the whole act if its core spending-limit sections fall [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks the money-in-politics problem on several fronts at once — PAC contributions, soft money, bundling, self-financing, disclosure — while offering candidates a genuine alternative through public financing and discounted ads. Its costs to taxpayers are small and voluntary, and its main design weakness is the independent-expenditure loophole, which it compensates for but does not close. The larger practical risk is constitutional, which the drafters acknowledged by writing in fast-track court review. On balance it is a coherent, if ambitious, reform whose main cost falls on the industries and actors currently dominating campaign money.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the Rules Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never reported it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Feingold introduced the Senate Campaign Financing and Spending Reform Act on January 21, 1997, with Senator Reid as cosponsor [S3][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration the same day [S5].
No further action was taken for the rest of the 105th Congress: no hearing, no committee report, no floor vote [S5].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, killing the bill [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent senators and the big-money channels around them — PACs, party soft-money operations, bundlers, and self-financing candidates — were better off, because the existing fundraising system they rely on stayed untouched. Ordinary voters lost the disclosure, spending limits, and small-donor incentives the bill would have created.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and the bill attracted no Republican cosponsors, and the Republican-chaired Rules Committee never acted on it; no floor vote was ever taken, so the broader party split was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill cuts PAC contributions to Senate candidates from $5,000 to $1,000 and caps total PAC money in a Senate race at $825,000, sharply shrinking PACs' role in Senate elections. PAC money is a primary channel through which organized economic interests buy access to senators.

industries.industry: Political party committees (national, congressional, and state)
industries.note: The bill bars national and congressional party committees from soliciting or spending soft money and forces state party spending affecting federal elections into regulated funds. Parties lose their main route around contribution limits.

The bill forces stations to sell candidate airtime at lower rates, including 50 percent off the lowest unit rate for participating Senate candidates, and bars preempting candidate ads. Broadcasters lose ad revenue that currently comes from unlimited campaign spending.

Personal and family campaign spending is capped at $25,000 per election cycle, ending the advantage of wealthy self-funded candidates. Their spending is also counted against any out-of-state contribution requirement.
Bundled contributions must be disclosed as coming through the bundler, and certain lobbyist fundraising and contributions are prohibited, raising the cost of the influence business.
